name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Standardize a one-page "Decision Log" template for every team to record every nontrivial choice, its reason, and the trade-off accepted. Product Ops owns it. The trade-off is upfront time to fill the log versus long-term clarity and faster onboarding.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that a one-page "Decision Log" template becomes another box-ticking exercise if Product Ops enforces it without tying it to actual decisions. Instead, mandate that every RFC or sprint plan must include a *decision section* in the existing artifact (e.g., Confluence page or Notion doc) with the same fields—no new template. Product Ops verifies compliance by checking the section exists, not by creating a new log. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot where teams use the section in their existing docs; if adoption stalls, revisit enforcement.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Scriv’s “decision section” in every RFC and sprint plan now. It forces teams to state the choice, the reason, and the trade-off at the moment the decision is made, not after the fact. The trade-off is a small upfront pause in writing versus the long-term clarity that prevents rehashing old choices and speeds up onboarding. Product Ops enforces the rule and reviews a random sample each sprint to keep it real.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s “decision section” in RFCs and sprint plans risks becoming a perfunctory checkbox unless Product Ops ties it to a concrete artifact teams must update *after* the decision lands. Instead, mandate a living “Decision Ledger” in Notion—one table where every nontrivial choice is logged with its reason, trade-off, and owner, updated by the decision-maker within 48 hours. The trade-off is a slight delay in execution versus a single source of truth that prevents rehashing and onboarding friction.

name: Scope
text: Adopt Scriv’s “decision section” in every RFC and sprint plan now. It forces teams to state the choice, the reason, and the trade-off at the moment the decision is made, not after the fact. The trade-off is a small upfront pause in writing versus the long-term clarity that prevents rehashing old choices. Product Ops owns enforcement and ties the section to the actual artifact teams update.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that a "decision section" in RFCs or sprint plans becomes a perfunctory checkbox unless Product Ops ties it to a concrete artifact teams must update *after* the decision lands. Instead, mandate a living "Decision Ledger" in Notion—one table where every nontrivial choice is logged with its reason and trade-off, and where the owner is forced to update it within 24 hours of the decision. That settles the argument: either the ledger exists and is used, or it doesn’t.

name: Reel
text: Adopt Scriv’s “decision section” in every RFC and sprint plan now. It forces teams to state the choice, the reason, and the trade-off at the moment the decision is made, not after the fact. The trade-off is a small upfront pause in writing versus the long-term clarity that prevents rehashing old choices. Product Ops owns enforcement and keeps the template lightweight to avoid box-ticking.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: A "Decision Ledger" in Notion risks becoming a dumping ground unless Product Ops enforces strict write-only access for the decision-maker and read-only for everyone else—otherwise, teams will game the system by retrofitting old choices. Instead, mandate that every RFC or sprint plan must include a *decision section* with a mandatory "revisit by" date; the artifact is the RFC/sprint page itself, and the lead is the author of the decision.

name: Chisel
text: Mandate a single "Decision Log" Slack channel where every nontrivial choice is posted within one hour of the decision, with the format: "We chose X because Y, accepting Z trade-off." Product Ops owns the channel and enforces the rule; anyone can post, but the decision-maker must sign their name. This forces immediate clarity without extra tools, but the trade-off is that some teams will resist the public accountability of a real-time feed.

name: Sift
text: Slack channels rot. Messages scroll, get buried, and break links—no one audits them later. A Notion Decision Ledger with a strict schema and Product Ops as editor forces structure and permanence. Settle it by building the Notion table first, then measure how often teams reference it in retrospectives.

name: Scope
text:
Build a Notion Decision Ledger now. Every RFC and sprint plan must include a linked entry in this table before the work starts, with columns for the choice, reason, trade-off, decision-maker, and date. Product Ops owns the schema and enforces completion—no entry, no approval.

Trade-off: Teams lose 10 minutes of upfront time to fill the table, but we gain a single source of truth that stops endless debates about past choices.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: A Notion Decision Ledger tied to RFCs and sprint plans risks becoming a bureaucratic gatekeeping exercise—teams will fill it with boilerplate to pass approval, not real reasoning. Instead, mandate a lightweight "Decision Summary" in the existing RFC template: one paragraph under a heading, signed by the decision-maker, with no extra tooling. Settle it by tracking how often these summaries are referenced in retrospectives for three sprints.

name: Reel
text: Build a Notion Decision Ledger now, with Product Ops owning the schema and enforcement. Every RFC and sprint plan must link to a pre-filled entry before work starts—columns for choice, reason, trade-off, decision-maker, and date. This forces clarity at the point of decision, not after the fact, and creates a permanent artifact teams can audit later. Trade-off: Teams lose 10 minutes per plan to fill the entry, but gain hours saved from rehashing old choices.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Notion Decision Ledger risks becoming a compliance checkbox—teams will paste boilerplate to clear RFC gates, not to record real trade-offs. Instead, mandate a one-sentence "decision summary" in the RFC template, signed by the decision-maker, and audit it in retrospectives for actual impact. Settle it by measuring how often teams reference these summaries in post-mortems versus Notion entries.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt a hybrid rule: every RFC and sprint plan must include a one-sentence “decision summary” signed by the decision-maker, and Product Ops must audit these summaries in retrospectives for real-world impact. This keeps reasoning visible without adding a heavy ledger, and it forces teams to state trade-offs up front instead of after the fact. The trade-off is that some summaries will be thin at first, but the retrospective audits will quickly expose weak entries and push quality up.

name: Sift
text: The hybrid rule risks creating two weak signals instead of one strong one: the one-sentence summary will be too vague to audit, and the retrospective check will be too late to matter. Instead, mandate a *short* but *structured* decision section in the RFC template—three bullet points: choice, key trade-off, and decision-maker—signed off by Product Ops before work starts. Settle it by measuring how often teams reference these sections in retrospectives and whether they actually influence future decisions.
